title: Boiling Down Argument: Five Approaches to Teaching Argument
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart argues that after deciding to teach argument as the heart of critical thinking across the content areas, teachers must first settle what argument actually is. Because standards from Common Core to NGSS invoke argument without defining it, he suspects most secondary teachers could not give an actionably clear definition, and students inherit that fuzziness. He surveys five frameworks: Graff and Birkenstein's They Say/I Say, Les Lynn's five components, Toulmin's four-part model, Erik Palmer's deliberately simple definition, and Jennifer Fletcher's rhetorical threshold skills. The move is a working teacher's literature review rather than a verdict, and he openly admits that each reduction loses something. He closes by positioning pop-up debates as the simple first step and committing to dig deeper into these approaches to raise the quality of written argument.
points: Standards demand argument everywhere yet rarely define it, so a teacher's first job is to build a clear, shared definition before teaching it.
Graff and Birkenstein teach argument through explicit sentence templates built on summarizing what others say and then responding, while Lynn adapts the same core for K-12 use.
Toulmin's model (claim, evidence, warrant and backing, counterargument) is the version embedded in Common Core, so its classroom implications are worth understanding directly.

Palmer accepts that simplifying argument loses nuance and argues teachers of adolescents should not be purists; Fletcher counters that rhetorical reading and writing are the threshold skills underneath argument.
Pop-up debates remain the entry point for raising the volume of spoken argument, which then feeds improvement in written argument.
quotes: This poses a teaching challenge, of course, because when the teacher doesn’t clearly understand something, you can bet that many of the students won’t. So, what are the most effective means for conceptualizing what argument is and teaching students to improve at it?
Importantly, Graff and Birkenstein teach students these skills through the use of explicit sentence templates. See their book, They Say, I Say, for these things and more.

And here we run into the central trouble with reducing anything, be it critical thinking or debate: with every reduction, something is lost. Argument purists would likely find fault in Palmer’s formulation, but Palmer’s primary concern in Good Thinking is, unsurprisingly, helping our students to think better.

Specifically, Fletcher calls for learning experiences that strengthen student mastery of the rhetorical concepts of occasion, audience, purpose, ethos, pathos, and logos. This rhetorical approach to teaching arguments, Fletcher argues, helps students form responses to texts that go beyond the superficial.

To be clear, I still see pop-up debates as Step One. I still think they are the simplest means for getting kids on their feet and arguing. They help us to increase the volume of spoken argument, which in turn gives us so many segues into improving the quality of written argument.
